title: Humanoid Robots in 2026: What They Do and Cost
seoTitle: Humanoid Robots 2026: Prices, Specs and Availability
excerpt: Humanoid robots in 2026 are still mostly in pilots. See what they can do, real prices, specs, and who can actually buy one.
content:
Are Humanoid Robots Available to Buy in 2026?

The headline humanoid robots of 2026 are not yet consumer products. Tesla Optimus, Figure 03 and Boston Dynamics Atlas have no published price and no public order page. Tesla uses Optimus internally and says public sales should begin by the end of 2027. Figure works with business partners only, and every Atlas built in 2026 is committed to Hyundai and Google DeepMind. A smaller set of machines, mainly from Unitree and 1X, does carry public prices, but they are farther from the general-purpose helpers the industry promises.

What Can a Humanoid Robot Actually Do?

Today's humanoids can walk on two legs, climb stairs, carry objects and repeat simple sequences in controlled settings. They use cameras and sensors to map a room, avoid obstacles and recognise items, then plan a route or a manipulation sequence. Advanced systems such as Figure's Helix model combine vision and language so the robot can respond to spoken instructions. What they cannot yet do is handle arbitrary household tasks with the reliability of a person. Dexterity remains limited, fine motor work is slow, and most units need frequent recharging.

How Much Do Humanoid Robots Cost?

No published price exists for Tesla Optimus, Figure 03, Boston Dynamics Atlas, Agility Digit 5 or Apptronik Apollo 2. Elon Musk has said Optimus might cost $20,000 to $30,000 at scale, but that is a cost target, not a price you can pay. Among machines with real list prices, Unitree's R1 starts at $4,900, the G1 at $13,500 and the H2 at $29,900, while 1X's NEO home robot is listed at $20,000 or $499 a month with a refundable deposit. A price tracker updated 13 November 2026 puts the median humanoid at $13,500. Prices say little about capability: a $5,000 unit and a $30,000 unit differ sharply in payload, runtime and balance.

Who Makes the Best-Known Humanoids?

Tesla, Figure AI and Boston Dynamics dominate coverage, but they are not the only players. Unitree sells small humanoids online at public prices. Agility Robotics targets warehouse work with Digit, and Apptronik builds Apollo for industrial customers. Chinese manufacturers including AGIBOT and UBTECH sell walking robots to businesses. The field splits broadly into research platforms, low-cost hobby machines and enterprise pilots, each with a different buyer and a different definition of useful.

What Are the Specs of the Leading Models?

Figure 03 stands 173 cm tall, weighs 61 kg, carries a 20 kg payload and runs for about five hours. It has cameras in its palms and fingertip sensors that detect forces as small as three grams, with washable coverings and 2 kW wireless charging. Boston Dynamics' electric Atlas, unveiled in product form at CES in January 2026, is 1.9 m tall, weighs 90 kg, has 56 degrees of freedom and can lift 50 kg, swapping its own batteries. Tesla has published no spec sheet; the widely repeated 173 cm, 57 kg and 20 kg payload figures come from presentations and are announced targets, not confirmed specifications.

Are Humanoid Robots Safe in the Home?

Safety is the main reason manufacturers keep humanoids out of homes. A machine that walks among people, children and pets must stop instantly when something enters its path. Builders use force-limited joints, collision detection and software speed caps, alongside emergency stop buttons and sensor arrays. Independent certification for home use is still emerging, and insurers have limited actuarial data on robots that move autonomously. Until standards settle, the safest applications remain factories and research labs where the environment is controlled and people keep their distance.

How Do Humanoids Differ from Industrial Robots?

A conventional industrial robot is bolted to a floor, repeats one precise motion and works behind a safety cage. A humanoid walks, uses the same tools and doorways as a person, and is meant to adapt to spaces that were never engineered for machines. That flexibility is the whole point, and the whole difficulty. Fixed robots are fast, cheap and reliable at one job. Humanoids trade that reliability for the ability to attempt many jobs in places built for people.

Where Are Humanoids Being Used Now?

Early deployment is concentrated in warehousing, manufacturing and research. Figure works with commercial partners on factory floors. Boston Dynamics has committed its 2026 Atlas units to Hyundai's manufacturing operations and Google DeepMind, which is bringing its Gemini Robotics models to the platform. Agility's Digit is being trialled for material handling. Tesla uses Optimus inside its own facilities for data collection. Home use remains a roadmap item rather than a shipping product.

What Are the Limitations of Current Humanoids?

Battery life is short, typically one to five hours, and many robots need to pause work to recharge. Balance on uneven ground is fragile, so stairs and clutter slow them down. Hands lack the fine motor control for tasks such as buttoning a shirt or handling a fragile glass. Speech understanding has improved but still misreads accents and ambiguous requests. Cost is the final barrier: a machine that needs a service contract and a specialist operator cannot compete with a human on most jobs.

How Are Humanoid Robots Maintained?

Humanoids need regular calibration of sensors and joints, software updates and occasional replacement of wear parts such as actuators and hand fingertips. Enterprise customers typically sign service contracts that cover diagnostics and repairs. Software arrives over the network, much like a phone update, and can add capabilities between hardware revisions. Owners should expect downtime, because these are early machines with moving parts under load.

In India

India has no local list price for a humanoid robot, and no Indian manufacturer sells a general-purpose model at a published rupee price. Buyers importing a Unitree G1 at $13,500 face customs duty, GST and shipping on top of the converted cost, so the landed price can run well above the sticker. At an indicative exchange rate of about ₹88 to the dollar, $13,500 is roughly ₹11.9 lakh before taxes and duties; the exact figure depends on the rate on the day of purchase and the customs classification. For Indian businesses, the more realistic route is leasing or robotics-as-a-service, where a provider owns the hardware and charges for uptime. Companies such as AgiBot and Agility have explored that model, according to their published materials. Universities and research institutes in India are the most likely early buyers, using humanoids for teaching and automation studies rather than factory work.

In Other Countries

The United States leads in funding and prototypes, with Tesla, Figure, Agility and Apptronik all based there, and most enterprise pilots running on American factory floors. China has the broadest catalogue of orderable machines: Unitree, AGIBOT, UBTECH and others sell humanoids that can be delivered today, often at lower prices than Western rivals. Europe has focused on research and regulation, with strong robotics labs in Germany and the UK but fewer commercial humanoid products. The UK's health and safety framework makes workplace trials slow, while Gulf states have begun buying humanoids for hospitality experiments.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I buy a humanoid robot in 2026?

Yes, but only a few. Unitree sells models online from $4,900 and 1X takes pre-orders for NEO. Tesla, Figure and Boston Dynamics do not sell to the public.

Why is Tesla Optimus not for sale?

Tesla uses Optimus internally and has published no price or order page. Musk has said public sales should begin by the end of 2027.

How much does a humanoid robot cost?

Orderable models run from $4,900 to $29,900. The headline machines from Tesla, Figure and Boston Dynamics have no public price at all.

How long do humanoid robot batteries last?

Most current models run for one to five hours before recharging, depending on the task and how much they walk and lift.

Will humanoids replace workers soon?

Unlikely in the near term. Early machines are slow, need specialist maintenance and cost more than a worker for most tasks. Factory pilots are expanding, but broad replacement is years away.
